author: David Sackrider
title: Judge blocks $1M in state funding for Jackson Field - NewsBreak
text:
By David Sackrider ,
3 hours ago
LANSING, Mich. (WLNS) — A Court of Claims judge has blocked $1 million in state funding for Jackson Field, home of the Lansing Lugnuts.
The funds were appropriated to the City of Lansing, who owns the field, as part of the 2024-25 budget. The Mackinac Center for Public Policy, a conservative think tank, sued the state last year, arguing the legislature did not follow the constitution when they passed that budget.
Attorney Patrick Wright said the lawsuit was not intended to target America’s pastime.
Patrick Wright, VP for Legal Affairs at the Mackinac Center for Public Policy. (WLNS) “I had a wonderful experience as a kid playing it. Saw Little League All-Star teams, loved going to the games, things of that nature. It just so happened that they were easy to isolate,” said Wright.
Wright is the Vice President for Legal Affairs at the Mackinac Center, which is focused on Article IV Sec. 30 of the Michigan Constitution.
That section states that a supermajority is necessary to spend state money for “local or private” purposes. However, the budget was only approved by two votes in the House of Representatives and four in the Senate back in 2024.
“By having this threshold of two thirds of each chamber be so high, the theory is that you are going to get less of this earmarks or pork,” Wright said.
Jackson Field in Lansing, home of the Lansing Lugnuts. (WLNS) He added that they did not want to undo the more than $1 billion in local projects inside the state budget. That’s why they started with two small ones, Jimmy John’s Field in Utica, and Jackson Field in Lansing.
“What we really did want to do is make sure in the future that this practice would be respected,” Wright said.
Attorneys for the state argued that Jackson Field serves a nonlocal purpose, benefiting the entire state, according to the order released by the Court of Claims.
“This is a public use,” said Lansing Mayor Andy Schor. “This is something where we get people from all over the region, all over the state who come to that field.”
Lansing Mayor Andy Schor. (WLNS) Schor says the funds would be used to make improvements that they simply do not have enough room for the city’s budget.
“It’s always difficult to put money into a ballpark when you want to deal with public safety or you want to deal with roads and sidewalks and infrastructure,” he said.
Judge Michael Gadola took the side of the Mackinac Center to block the funds, writing that there is “a compelling argument” the funds were for the city’s benefit — not the state’s.
The order is a preliminary injunction, not a final decision. The funds will be put on pause while the court continues to hear the case. They could still decide to rule in the favor of the state and allow the grant to flow to Jackson Field.
In the meantime, Mayor Schor told 6 News that he hopes the Attorney General’s office will appeal the decision to issue a preliminary injunction.
